metric.why: A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks; airflow and pressure sensors find recirculation, bypass, and leaks that temperature averages hide.
metric.definition: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.

reading.body:
Airflow and static pressure expose cooling failures that temperature readings miss, revealing recirculation, bypass, and leaks that can starve racks of cold air even when a facility's total cooling capacity appears adequate.

A data center can deliver enough cubic feet per minute to the room while that air never reaches the equipment that needs it. Static pressure measurements show whether air moves through racks or takes the path of least resistance around them. This gap between total capacity and actual delivery explains why two facilities with identical temperature sensors and identical cooling systems can have radically different performance under load.

For AI workloads that concentrate extreme power density in small spaces, this metric matters more than it does for traditional computing. A GPU cluster pulling 500 kilowatts per cabinet generates heat faster than the room's average temperature can signal a problem. Pressure differentials catch the failure before temperatures spike and shut down chips.

This metric does not measure the efficiency of the cooling system itself, the cost of the power used to move the air, or whether the static pressure target is correctly set for a given facility's layout and equipment. It captures one point in time and cannot predict failure. But for operators trying to understand why their highest-performance racks underperform, it reveals what thermometers alone cannot.
